# 2 Kings Chapter 6 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 227r–228r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2KI_006_page_001.jpg, 2KI_006_page_002.jpg, 2KI_006_page_003.jpg

---

**1** The company of prophets said to Elisha, "The place where we meet with you has become too small for us.

**2** Let us go to the Jordan, and each of us will get a log, and we'll build ourselves a new meeting place there." "Go ahead," he said.

**3** Then one of them said, "Please come with us." "I'll come," he replied.

**4** So he went with them. When they reached the Jordan, they began cutting down trees.

**5** As one of them was chopping a beam, the iron axe head flew off and sank into the water. "Oh no, my master!" he cried. "It was borrowed!"

**6** "Where did it fall?" the man of God asked. When the man showed him the spot, Elisha cut a stick, threw it into the water, and the iron axe head floated to the surface.

**7** "Grab it," he said. The man reached out and picked it up.

**8** Now the king of Aram was at war with Israel. He would consult with his officers and say, "We'll set up camp at such-and-such a location."

**9** But each time, the man of God would send a warning to the king of Israel: "Stay away from that area — the Arameans are heading there."

**10** So the king of Israel would send scouts to the place the man of God indicated. Time after time Elisha warned him, and he stayed on guard.

**11** This infuriated the king of Aram. He summoned his officers and demanded, "Tell me! Which of you is leaking information to the king of Israel?"

**12** "None of us, my lord," one officer said. "It's Elisha, the prophet in Israel. He tells the king of Israel the very words you speak in your own bedroom."

**13** "Go find out where he is," the king ordered, "so I can send men to capture him." The report came back: "He's in Dothan."

**14** So the king sent a strong force — horses, chariots, and a large army — and they arrived at night and surrounded the city.

**15** When Elisha's servant got up early the next morning and went outside, he saw the army with horses and chariots encircling the city. "Oh, my master!" he cried. "What are we going to do?"

**16** "Don't be afraid," Elisha answered. "Those who are with us outnumber those who are with them."

**17** Then Elisha prayed, "LORD, open his eyes so he can see." The LORD opened the servant's eyes, and he looked up and saw the hills blazing with horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.

**18** As the Aramean army advanced toward him, Elisha prayed, "LORD, strike these people with blindness." And the LORD struck them blind, just as Elisha had asked.

**19** Then Elisha went out to them and said, "This isn't the right road, and this isn't the right city. Follow me — I'll take you to the man you're looking for." And he led them straight into Samaria.

**20** Once they were inside Samaria, Elisha prayed, "LORD, open their eyes so they can see." The LORD opened their eyes — and they found themselves standing in the middle of Samaria.

**21** When the king of Israel saw them, he asked Elisha eagerly, "Shall I kill them? Shall I kill them, my father?"

**22** "No!" Elisha said. "You don't execute prisoners of war you didn't even capture yourself. Give them food and water, let them eat and drink, and send them back to their master."

**23** So the king prepared a huge feast for them. After they had eaten and drunk their fill, he sent them home to their master. And the Aramean raiders never came into Israelite territory again.

**24** Some time later, King Ben-hadad of Aram assembled his entire army and marched up to besiege Samaria.

**25** The siege caused a terrible famine. Things got so bad that a donkey's head sold for eighty pieces of silver, and a cup of seed pods for five.

**26** One day, as the king of Israel was walking along the city wall, a woman shouted to him, "Help me, my lord the king!"

**27** "If the LORD won't help you," he snapped, "where am I supposed to get help for you? From an empty threshing floor? From a dry winepress?"

**28** Then the king asked, "What's the matter?" She said, "This woman made a deal with me: 'Let's eat your son today and mine tomorrow.'

**29** So we cooked my son and ate him. The next day I said to her, 'Now give up your son so we can eat him.' But she'd hidden her son."

**30** When the king heard the woman's words, he tore his robes. As he continued along the wall, the people could see that underneath his royal garments he was wearing sackcloth against his skin.

**31** He declared, "May God strike me dead if the head of Elisha son of Shaphat stays on his shoulders by the end of today!"

**32** Meanwhile, Elisha was sitting in his house with the city elders. The king had sent a man ahead, but before the messenger even arrived, Elisha said to the elders, "Do you see? This murderer's son has sent someone to cut off my head. When the messenger gets here, shut the door and brace it against him. His master is right behind him."

**33** While Elisha was still speaking, the messenger arrived. And the king said, "This disaster is from the LORD himself! Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?"

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 5 — "It was borrowed!":** This seemingly minor detail packs a punch. These prophets were so poor they couldn't afford their own tools. Losing a borrowed iron axe head was both financially devastating and socially humiliating. The miracle of the floating iron shows God's care for the small, everyday crises of ordinary people — not just the grand dramas of kings and armies.

**Verse 17 — The unseen army:** One of the most vivid images in all of Scripture. The visible threat (an encircling army) is real. But the invisible reality (a mountain blazing with heavenly fire) is more real. This passage has shaped how believers think about spiritual reality for millennia.

**Verse 22-23 — Feeding the enemy:** Elisha's ethics are revolutionary. Instead of slaughtering a blinded, helpless enemy, he throws them a feast. The result is more effective than any military victory — the raids stop. This is ancient Israel's most striking example of defeating enemies through unexpected generosity.

**Verse 28-29 — The cannibalism:** The narrative shifts from miracle stories to the darkest depths of human desperation. The siege has pushed Samaria past civilizational collapse. This scene deliberately echoes the curses of Deuteronomy 28:53-57 — what Moses warned would happen if Israel broke covenant.

**Verse 33 — "Why should I wait for the LORD?":** The chapter ends on a note of raw theological crisis. The king stands at the breaking point between faith and despair. He has been wearing sackcloth (a sign of desperate prayer), but the prayers haven't worked. His patience — and his theology — have shattered.

*— PNEUMA*
